title: South Korea Boosts Growth Outlook, hikes Benchmark Rate to Two‑Year High, CNBC Reports
body:
Seoul’s monetary authority lifted its policy rate by a quarter‑point on Thursday, taking the benchmark lending rate to 3.25 percent – the highest level the country has seen since early 2022. The move, announced at the bank’s final policy meeting of 2024, was broadly anticipated by analysts who had been tracking a gradual tightening cycle aimed at re‑anchoring inflation that has persistently hovered above the central bank’s 2 percent target. By raising rates while simultaneously upgrading its growth outlook, the Bank of Korea signalled confidence that a resilient domestic economy can absorb tighter financial conditions without slipping into recession.

The decision follows a series of data releases that painted a picture of a still‑robust Korean economy. Gross domestic product expanded by 3.6 percent year‑on‑year in the first three quarters, outpacing most of its regional peers. Export volumes, buoyed by strong demand for semiconductors and automotive components, continued to climb, while consumer spending recovered after a modest dip in early 2024. At the same time, the consumer price index eased only marginally, staying at 2.8 percent in September – well above the central bank’s target band and above the 2.5 percent threshold that would have allowed a pause in rate hikes. The dual pressures of a buoyant economy and stubborn price growth left policymakers with limited leeway.

Economists had largely expected a 25‑basis‑point increase, but the upgrade to the growth forecast was a surprise element that underscored the bank’s optimism. The new projection of 2.8 percent annual GDP growth for 2024, up from the previously forecast 2.5 percent, reflects expectations that the recovery in global demand for high‑tech goods will sustain Korea’s export‑driven engine. Moreover, the labor market remains tight, with unemployment at a 15‑month low of 2.6 percent and wage growth edging higher. These factors reduce the risk of a demand‑side slowdown even as borrowing costs rise.

The rate hike also marks a divergence from several of Korea’s major trading partners, many of which have either held rates steady or begun easing amid slowing global growth. While the United States Federal Reserve is expected to maintain its policy range through year‑end, the European Central Bank has signalled a more cautious stance. By moving ahead of this regional trend, the Bank of Korea aims to pre‑empt any inflationary spill‑over from a still‑tight labor market and from imported price pressures, particularly in energy and raw materials. Critics warn that a higher cost of credit could dampen investment in small‑ and medium‑sized enterprises, which rely heavily on bank financing, and could strain households already coping with rising housing prices.

Market participants reacted swiftly. The won appreciated modestly against the dollar, gaining roughly 0.4 percent in early trade, as investors priced in a more hawkish monetary outlook. Domestic bond yields rose, with the 10‑year government bond moving up 5 basis points to 3.45 percent, reflecting higher borrowing costs for the public sector. Analysts at major Korean banks expect the tightening cycle to conclude by early 2025, provided inflation shows a clear downward trajectory. However, they caution that any external shock – such as a slowdown in Chinese demand or renewed geopolitical tensions in the region – could force the central bank to reassess its stance.

Looking ahead, the Bank of Korea’s next steps will hinge on the interplay between price stability and growth sustainability. If inflation begins to converge toward the 2 percent target without a corresponding dip in economic momentum, the central bank may hold rates steady through the first half of 2025 before considering a gradual easing. Conversely, a resurgence of price pressures or a sharp external downturn could compel further tightening, testing the resilience of households and businesses alike. For now, the 3.25 percent rate serves as both a signal of confidence in Korea’s economic engine and a reminder that the path to price stability remains a delicate balancing act.
